finding.question: What federal income tax amounts did Donald Trump report or pay in the years associated with the $750 figure, and what other taxes are excluded from that figure?
finding.summary: Reporting based on Trump’s tax-return data found $750 in federal income tax liability for each of 2016 and 2017. The figure was the income tax due before withholding and prepayments, not merely a final payment or filing fee. Trump had made extension payments of $1 million for 2016 and $4.2 million for 2017; most was rolled forward toward potential future taxes. The $750 figure excludes other taxes, such as Social Security and Medicare taxes, property and sales taxes, and state taxes.

finding.summary: In the 2016 presidential debate, Hillary Clinton said that records Trump submitted for a casino license showed he had paid no federal income tax in certain years. Trump interrupted: “That makes me smart.” He did not say the quoted wording in that exchange. In a separate 2020 debate, he defended using tax laws, saying, “I don't want to pay tax” and that private individuals, “unless they're stupid,” go through the laws; the attributed quotation appears to paraphrase such remarks rather than reproduce his words verbatim.

report_raw.claim: Why should you pay more taxes than Donald Trump pays? And that’s a fact. $750. Remember what he said when that was raised a while ago, how he only pays … He said, ‘Because I’m smart. I know how to game the system.’
report_raw.justification: Reporting based on Trump’s tax-return data put his federal income tax liability at $750 in both 2016 and 2017, before withholding and prepayments were applied. [S1][S2] The figure does not represent all taxes, and a Tax Policy Center model estimated that about half of U.S. tax units paid more than $750 in federal income tax in those years. [S3][S4][S5] But the attributed quotation is not what Trump said in the identified 2016 debate exchange: after Hillary Clinton raised years in which he paid no federal income tax, he replied, “That makes me smart.” [S8][S9] Inference: The claim is refuted because it presents a paraphrase as an exact quotation, although its tax comparison is substantially supported for many taxpayers.
key_points: The $750 figure refers to federal income tax liability in each of 2016 and 2017, not to all taxes or merely the balance paid at filing. [S1][S2][S3][S4]
An estimated half of U.S. tax units paid more than $750 in federal income tax in those years; this does not establish what any individual paid. [S5]
Trump’s recorded 2016 words were “That makes me smart,” not the quotation attributed to him in the claim. [S8][S9]
The evidence does not rule out Trump using the attributed wording on some other occasion. [S8][S9][S10]
report_raw.counter_argument: A case for a less negative verdict is that the $750 figure is supported, many taxpayers paid more, and Trump’s actual remarks convey a similar idea about using tax laws intelligently. [S1][S2][S5][S8][S10] That does not prevail because the claim presents particular words as a direct quotation, and they do not match the identified exchange. [S8][S9]
evidence_gaps: The underlying tax returns were not publicly released as of the reference date; the $750 figures rely on reporting based on tax-return data.
The available sources do not establish a complete total for Trump’s other taxes.
The identified debate transcripts do not conclusively establish whether Trump used the attributed wording on another occasion.

findings.question: What federal income tax amounts did Donald Trump report or pay in the years associated with the $750 figure, and what other taxes are excluded from that figure?
findings.summary: Reporting based on Trump’s tax-return data found $750 in federal income tax liability for each of 2016 and 2017. The figure was the income tax due before withholding and prepayments, not merely a final payment or filing fee. Trump had made extension payments of $1 million for 2016 and $4.2 million for 2017; most was rolled forward toward potential future taxes. The $750 figure excludes other taxes, such as Social Security and Medicare taxes, property and sales taxes, and state taxes.

But virtually all of that liability was washed away when he eventually filed, and most of the payments were rolled forward to cover potential taxes in future years. ... findings.question: How does the relevant $750 federal income tax figure compare with federal income tax paid or owed by typical U.S. taxpayers in the same years?
findings.summary: The Tax Policy Center estimated that about half of U.S. tax units paid more than $750 in federal income tax in 2016 and 2017. Separately, the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Consumer Expenditure Survey estimated that the average U.S. household paid $8,367 in federal income taxes in 2016. These measures indicate that many people paid more than the reported $750, but they cannot establish what any particular audience member paid.

sources.title: Donald Trump paid $750 in income tax in 2017. About half of Americans paid more.
sources.snippet: Mark Mazur, the director of the Tax Policy Center (America’s leading nonpartisan tax think tank) and a former assistant secretary for tax policy at the Treasury Department, told me that according to TPC’s models, about half of American tax units* paid more than $750 in federal income taxes in 2016 and 2017.

sources.title: Donald Trump Taxes vs. Average American Income Tax Payment
sources.snippet: According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Expenditure Survey, the average U.S. household paid $8,367 in federal income taxes in 2016.

sources.title: How much the average American pays in taxes each year
sources.snippet: Like the $750 figure for Trump, they also do not include payroll taxes like Social Security and Medicare. Around 44% of U.S. households do not pay any individual federal income taxes, according to the TPC.

caveats: A tax unit can differ from a household, and the reported household average is not a median; high-income households can raise the average.
The Tax Policy Center comparison is a model estimate, not a count of actual returns. Federal income tax is distinct from payroll and other taxes.

findings.question: Did Donald Trump say, 'Because I’m smart. I know how to game the system,' in response to a question or allegation about how much tax he paid, and what were his exact words and their context?
findings.summary: In the 2016 presidential debate, Hillary Clinton said that records Trump submitted for a casino license showed he had paid no federal income tax in certain years. Trump interrupted: “That makes me smart.” He did not say the quoted wording in that exchange. In a separate 2020 debate, he defended using tax laws, saying, “I don't want to pay tax” and that private individuals, “unless they're stupid,” go through the laws; the attributed quotation appears to paraphrase such remarks rather than reproduce his words verbatim.

sources.title: Transcript: The Last Word with Lawrence O'Donnell, September 28, 2020
sources.snippet:
HILLARY CLINTON (D), FORMER PRESIDENTIAL CANDIDATE: The only years that anybody has ever seen were a couple of years when he had to turn them over to state authorities when he was trying to get a casino license and they showed he didn’t pay any federal income tax. So, if he paid —

TRUMP: That makes me smart.

(END VIDEO CLIP)

sources.snippet:

>
